doc.title: Chico Freeman interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001

title: Following his own voice and the Miles Davis trumpet sound
summary: His father taught him individuality; Miles Davis and Kind of Blue shaped his sound, and his college trumpet teacher dismissed Miles.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Yes, I say sorta kinda. I went through grammar school and high school and I was a little bit of a maverick you might say, a bit of a nonconformist in a way. My father had always taught me to follow my own voice, myself. That is a very, very strong concept that I think has always pervaded throughout this music. You know, particularly in the history of it. That the individual, the individuality and the originality is very important I think to the character of jazz. And so my father had always encouraged me to do that. And when I was playing the trumpet, I kind of got — there was one trumpet player that just got in my ear, and I couldn’t get him out. I mean I loved him there, it was a pleasant thing, but as I was playing that’s the only sound — I couldn’t really get next to the other trumpet players in terms of tone. And that trumpet player was Miles Davis. I just had an affinity for him. I had seen, my father played with Miles Davis and John Coltrane when I was like five years old. And I don’t know, and then the first record that I ever heard that made me decide that I wanted to be a musician and play music — and play jazz music I should say — it was “Kind of Blue,” so Miles Davis. And then the next trumpet player after him that I liked the tone-wise was Nat Adderley. So they had the type of tone, you know that dark, brooding kind of, because Nat played cornet really, so he had a darker sound. Now the other trumpet players, like Freddie Hubbard and Lee Morgan and Clifford Brown, they all had great sounds but they were very big and more brassy kind of sound. And I wasn’t into the marching band type of trumpet sound. So my big influence was Miles Davis. And I was trying to get that kind of sound. And I ran into some problems when I went to college with the classical teachers there. Because their concept of sound was completely different. And it really sort of got to me when I had — I loved this teacher — I had this trumpet teacher and I liked him. He was a nice guy. And he was trying to teach me. And I guess because he was so nice I wasn’t so belligerent, I was more trying to be persuasive and explain to him about what I was hearing and see if there was a way that he could help me achieve those goals in addition or alongside or something. And he really didn’t have the information or the vision to do that. So I tried to help him do that. So I went and bought him a bunch of Miles Davis records. And he came back and oh he just told me Miles Davis played out of tune and this, that. He just completely dissed Miles Davis.
